paper_title: Towards Physically Grounded Articulated 3D Assets: A Multi-Agent Pipeline and Benchmark

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In this paper, we study physically grounded articulated 3D asset generation---moving the goal from reproducing how objects look to capturing how they move and function. Inspired by the literature on procedural and agentic generation, we present Artisan, a system that extends the latest method Articraft by introducing a multi-agent pipeline with physical simulation feedback, enabling comprehensive attributes beyond geometry, appearance, and physically plausible articulation, such as collision-free motion, stability under gravity, and accurate mass and material properties. Furthermore, we construct a unified benchmark spanning four key aspects: spatial fidelity, physical plausibility, downstream task performance, and overall quality. The benchmark encompasses 100 reference assets from ArtVIP and LightWheel, 50 stability prompts, and 50 ABO objects with reference masses, with protocols evaluating various metrics. Through extensive evaluation of more than 10 representative models, Artisan achieves competitive spatial fidelity while attaining the lowest collision rates and highest stability rates among the evaluated methods. Together, our system and benchmark establish insights for advancing 3D generation towards physically plausible, functionally usable assets.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: We consider the problem of generating physically grounded articulated 3D assets from natural language and, optionally, reference images. Specifically, we aim to reconstruct the objects appearance and geometry, as well as structural, functional, and physical properties such as part hierarchies, joints, and mass. The intent is to capture the configuration space of the object and to support simulation of contact and gravity. By solving this problem, we can reduce the cost of creating assets for physics simulation (Genesis Authors, 2024; Genesis AI Team, 2026), product design (Willis et al., 2021), and robotics (Li et al., 2023; Nasiriany et al., 2026). Appearance, shape, articulation, and physical attributes are interdependent and should be modeled holistically. However, most existing methods address these properties separately, focusing on shape and appearance (Xiang et al., 2025; Hunyuan3D et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025c), articulation (Wu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a;b), or specific physical properties, such as materials (Wu et al., 2025b; Youwang et al., 2026), mass (Zhai et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2026a;b; Li et al., 2026c), stability (Chen et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2025), and collision-free motion (Luo et al., 2025; Kreber & Stueckler, 2025). Addressing each aspect in isolation makes it difficult to satisfy all of them, resulting in artifacts and defects in the reconstructions and ultimately limiting the usability of the generated assets. As alternatives to these learned models, procedural generators (Lian et al., 2025; Joshi et al., 2025) assemble assets programmatically, based on predefined rules that enforce desirable constraints and make at least some physical properties explicit and controllable. However, such rule-based systems limit the types of objects that can be generated and are difficult to use in tasks like image-based reconstruction. This limitation is addressed by several recently proposed agentic methods. For instance, Articraft (Zhou et al., 2026) uses Large Language Model (LLM) to write, validate, and revise programs that construct 3D objects, which is much more flexible than using canned rules of traditional procedural generators. However, Articraft and other similar approaches use single agent to both construct and verify the 3D program, which can lead to self-evaluation bias, where the agent may satisfy its own checks without genuinely ensuring the quality of the generated assets. Moreover, while their checks are meant to increase the likelihood that the generated assets would work in physics-simulated environment, the latter is not directly tested and may still fail. In this paper, we address these gaps by introducing ARTISAN, new pipeline that improves on the blueprint of Articraft (Zhou et al., 2026) by switching to multi-agent design and introducing physical simulator feedback. The new pipeline (Figure 2) consists of: (i) the Design Agent, which produces blueprint of the object specifying its parts, joints, and articulations; (ii) the Coding Agent, which translates the blueprint into program that outputs the geometry, articulations, and physical parameters of the object; and (iii) the Review Agent, which validates the built asset and provides feedback to the Coding Agent to revise the program. The agents work independently, exchanging only the blueprint, 3D asset, and feedback as explained. Their independence reduces the self-evaluation bias mentioned above. Furthermore, the validation step is augmented with feedback obtained from physical simulator, which verifies physical properties like collisions and stability within the target simulator environment. Existing benchmarks offer limited assessment of whether visual fidelity translates into physical plausibility and even functional usability to evaluate the assets produced by such pipelines. Our second key contribution is therefore to introduce new comprehensive benchmark that jointly assesses all of these properties. It evaluates: spatial fidelity, comparing the objects appearance, geometry, and kinematics to the reference inputs; physical attributes, measuring mass, material, stability under gravity, and collision under motion; downstream tasks, assessing the usability of the generated assets in tasks like robotic manipulation; and overall quality, based on human judgments after manipulating objects in the simulator. Each aspect is evaluated with multiple metrics. Using the new benchmark, we conduct extensive experiments to compare our method with state-ofthe-art models. Empirically, we find that the assets constructed by ARTISAN: (i) are faithful to the input references; (ii) are physically valid and articulate correctly; and (iii) work well in downstream tasks such as simulated robotic manipulation. We also show that ARTISAN outperforms the recent and strong models in most metrics and in human evaluation, especially improving physical properties like collision and stability. In most cases, our general-purpose pipeline is more accurate than task-specific feed-forward 3D reconstruction models. We also show that the constructed objects are functional and support downstream robotic manipulation tasks.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Creating Functional 3D Assets. Early methods build articulated objects through per-instance optimization (Mu et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022; Tseng et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Weng et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025a), but are limited to specific instances. To improve generalizability, learning-based methods create articulated objects from pure noise (Lei et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2025), text (Liu et al., 2024; Su et al., 2025), images (Liu et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2024a; He et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026b; Wu et al., 2026), videos (Delitzas et al., 2026) or 3D models (Li et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b), learning from large-scale datasets (Xiang et al., 2020; Li et al., 2026b). Recent methods focus on inferring independent physical properties from visual representations (Zhai et al., 2024; Shuai et al., 2025), jointly predicting these alongside joint motion characteristics (Cao et al., 2026a;b; Li et al., 2026c; Huang et al., 2026a), and leveraging simulation feedback to refine aspects such as support, clearances, or mobility (Chen et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Kreber & Stueckler, 2025; Xu et al., 2026). In contrast, ARTISAN generates articulated objects that take diverse physical properties into account. Procedural and Agentic 3D Asset Creation. Procedural systems construct editable and simulationready variations within the authored rules (Lian et al., 2025; Joshi et al., 2025). The latest agent-based pipelines extend this coverage through executable articulation, retrieval with visual critique, or semantic search over kinematic structures (Mandi et al., 2025; Le et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). Closer to our approach, Articraft (Zhou et al., 2026) builds articulated objects through an agent with Software Development Kit (SDK)s. Recent systems improve reliability through geometric and visual checks, and revisions to earlier construction stages when checks fail (Wang et al., 2026; Shui et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026). In contrast, ARTISAN introduces multi-agent pipeline with physical simulator feedback, enabling physically grounded articulated 3D asset generation. Datasets and Benchmarks for Physically Grounded 3D Assets. Articulated datasets provide part geometry and motion annotations (Xiang et al., 2020; Geng et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2022; Delitzas et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2026; Engelbracht et al., 2026). Program-generated collections further expand the available assets (Zhou et al., 2026; Cao et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026c). Existing benchmarks separately assess geometric and semantic fidelity (Li et al., 2026a; Duggal et al., 2025), programmatic modelling quality (Yang et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026), material properties (Cao et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026c), and motion behavior (Luo et al., 2025; Pham, 2026). Our benchmark comprehensively evaluates the spatial fidelity, physical plausibility, and downstream task utility of generated articulated assets using set of distinct metrics.

sections.title: 3.4 PHYSICAL VALIDATION
sections.content: We validate each candidate asset Ot through collision and stability checks in MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012). The resulting physics report Et records colliding part pairs and penetration depths at the tested joint configurations, together with tilt measurements under gravity, to guide coding and review. Collision under Motion. The collisions are determined based on whether different parts interpenetrate during the simulated motion sequences, across sampled configurations of single-joint, double-joint, and multi-joint motions (details in Appendix A.3). Specifically, we first perform convex decomposition (Wei et al., 2022) to construct mesh collision geometry for simulation. Then, we simulate the motion of each joint in isolation and record any collisions between parts. Collisions that persist during individual joint operation require remediation. Collision findings across motions include the affected part pairs, poses, and penetration depths, enabling the Review Agent to assess whether these collisions occur during normal operation (Section 3.3). Stability under Gravity. We simulate the assembly under gravity and measure its tilt angle relative to the initial pose to assess whether it remains upright. We run the MuJoCo simulation for up to 5 seconds under gravity. The 3D asset is considered unstable if it tilts beyond certain threshold during the simulation. The tilt measurements are recorded in Et for review against the intended use.

sections.title: 4 BENCHMARK
sections.content: A key contribution of our paper is to build comprehensive benchmark for physically grounded articulated 3D assets. To this end, we design set of evaluation protocols and metrics, and curate benchmark data with abundant annotations for these metrics.

sections.title: 4.1 EVALUATION PROTOCOL AND METRICS
sections.content: Spatial Fidelity. The spatial fidelity metrics evaluate how well the 3D shape of the generated asset matches the reference asset in both the rest-pose and the articulated states. We first perform point sampling and align the meshes using ICP registration (Besl & McKay, 1992), then establish correspondences between parts based on their centers using the Hungarian matching algorithm (Kuhn, 1955). Due to the difficulty of clearly distinguishing between states, outputs from different states may sometimes be confused. To avoid erroneous penalties, we test both state pairings and retain the one with the lower alignment error across the two states as the final aligned result. Appearance: After aligning the generated 3D asset to the reference asset, we render both using Blender at 10242 resolution from three viewpoints per state. We report the Intersection over Union (IoU) of the rendered masks, pixel-level PSNR, patch-level SSIM (Wang et al., 2004), feature-level LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018), and CLIP score (Radford et al., 2021) over all six images. Rest-Pose and Articulated Geometry: We calculate 3D metrics in both states. We report the object Chamfer Distance (oCD) for the object as whole. We also report the part-aware CD (pCD) and mean part IoU (pIoU) by averaging the metrics of all matched parts, following (Li et al., 2026a). Physical Properties. Except for spatial fidelity on appearance, geometric and kinematics, we also assess the physical properties of the generated assets, including the reconstructed materials and mass, the absence of collisions during articulated motion, and stability under gravity. Materials: Following PBR-NeRF (Wu et al., 2025b) and LMRM (Youwang et al., 2026), we evaluate the materials of the generated assets by rendering the colour, metallic, and roughness buffers from the same viewpoints used for appearance evaluation, and then calculating PSNR against corresponding renders of the reference asset. To mitigate the impact of geometric inconsistencies, we also develop protocol to transfer predicted materials to the ground-truth geometry so that the material attributes can be rendered and compared on the same geometry (results in Appendix Table 10). Mass: We compare the mass ˆm of the object against the corresponding ground-truth mass m. Here, we report three scores following (Standley et al., 2017; Zhai et al., 2024): ADE = ˆm in kilograms, APE = ˆm m/m and MnRE = min(r, 1/r), where = ˆm/m. Collision: We evaluate the collision of the generated asset at rest and during articulated motion. We sample the motion in three levels: single-joint, double-joint, and multi-joint. Specifically, for singlejoint motion, we uniformly sample 9 states ranging from the rest state to its (predicted) upper-limit state. For double-joint motion, we then combine two joints to form 9 9 grid of motion states. To efficiently evaluate multi-joint motion, we randomly sample state for each joint and perform total of 200 trials. To avoid penalizing collisions from joint combinations that violate motion dependencies, we establish joint correspondences using Hungarian matching (Kuhn, 1955), reproduce each sampled configuration on the ground-truth asset, and exclude colliding part pairs that also contact in that asset. At each sampling level, we report the percentage of collisions over all sampled states. Stability: Prior work (Guo et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025) evaluates stability under gravity primarily considering the whole object as single rigid body, with uniform mass distribution. We extend this evaluation to challenging benchmark of 50 articulated objects with high centers of mass. We simulate each object in MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012) for 10 seconds in both its rest and fully articulated states, and report the percentage of stable assets separately for each state. An object is considered stable if its maximum tilt angle relative to its initial pose remains below 30, its positional change is below 1 mm, and its rotational change does not exceed 0.01 rad. Robotic Task Performance. Beyond spatial fidelity and physical plausibility, we evaluate whether the generated assets are functionally usable and improve downstream task performance.

sections.title: 5 RESULTS
sections.content: 5.1 ANALYSIS OF BENCHMARK RESULTS Main Results. We compare ARTISAN to the state-of-the-art baselines described in Section 4.3. We show spatial fidelity results in Table 1 and Figure 4 and physical attribute results in Table 2 and Figure 5. Without bells and whistles, ours (GPT-6 Astra) outperforms the other methods in 8 of 11 metrics for spatial fidelity in Table 1. More importantly, it dramatically improves physical plausibility, reducing collision occurrences to 1.7% on single-joint and 13.0% on multi-joint evaluations, and achieving 98% and 96% stability in the rest and articulated states, respectively. This highlights the significant advantage of our method in generating physically grounded articulated assets. In the following, we summarize several key findings. More details are provided in Section C. Agentic generation methods can rival or even surpass state-of-the-art task-specific methods. Compared to very recent state-of-the-art task-specific model Instruct-Particulate, whose input mesh is generated by Hunyuan-3.1 (Tencent Hunyuan3D Team, 2026) from the reference image, our method consistently achieves superior results in most metrics in Tables 1 and 2. Figure 4 further illustrates the visual results in two additional reference-guided examples: motorcycle and miniature steam traction engine. Ours provides better appearance and articulated structure. sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented ARTISAN, pipeline that achieves physically grounded, articulated 3D asset generation by combining multiple agents and physical simulation feedback. We also introduced new comprehensive benchmark to evaluate various properties of the generated assets, including appearance, geometry, kinematics, materials, collision, mass, stability, and even robotic task performance. Empirically, we found that ARTISAN achieves the best overall performance across wide range of evaluation metrics, and even outperforms existing task-specific models in most areas. We also found that multi-agent harnessing with physical simulation feedback significantly improves the spatial and physical fidelity of the generated assets. Our findings motivate further research for our community: revisiting the role of feed-forward models, developing efficient agent harnesses across tasks, providing richer and more actionable simulator feedback, and extending simulators to capture broader range of physical phenomena. sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: Our human evaluation involves inspecting rendered assets and interacting with virtual objects in physics simulator, as described in Appendix B.4. Participants assess visual quality, articulation, and physical behavior through simulated interactions. We report aggregate preference statistics, and the supplementary offline demo contains no real participant data. The generated assets are intended for simulation and evaluation; their use in real-world robotic applications should undergo additional validation appropriate to the deployment setting.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 SDK EXTENSIONS Physical Property Abstraction. The SDK exposes three groups of physical attributes: part materials, part masses, and joint damping and friction. For materials, the Coding Agent selects named material preset and can directly adjust its PBR values, including albedo, metallicity, roughness, and opacity. For mass, the agent reasons from the blueprint to estimate each parts mass, considering its dimensions, materials, and construction. We deliberately avoid computing mass as material density times geometric volume, since real objects often combine multiple materials and contain hollow regions, making this approximation prone to large errors. The SDK computes each parts default inertia from its geometry and estimated mass. The agent can also adjust each parts inertial properties to reflect its mass distribution. Joint damping and friction are configured according to the motions and mechanisms specified in the blueprint. Standard Parts for Joint Connections. We provide six commonly used families of parameterized standard parts: hinges, slide rails, pinned joints, rotary connectors, telescoping slides, and threaded sleeves (Figure 3). Each connector is built from matching components with shared dimensions, alignment, and clearance parameters. For example, hinge halves share pin axis, while slide rail pairs guide with matching runner. The Coding Agent adapts their dimensions and mounting positions to the asset, reducing repeated geometric design and mismatches between mating components. Anchor-based Placement. Authoring every pose in explicit coordinates requires the agent to calculate distances and orientations, and to update them whenever geometry changes. We instead let the agent specify the intended spatial relationship and let the SDK solve the corresponding pose from the built geometry. An anchor names geometric feature on an existing element: an oriented plane from face, an axis from an edge or round features center line, or point from corner. Given subject anchor asub, reference anchors Aref , and placement parameters θ, the interface computes = ω(asub, Aref ; θ), where is the subjects rigid pose and θ specifies offsets, clearances, or translation direction. Common operations are ω {ATTACH, CENTRE, SNAP}: ATTACH aligns mating anchors with the requested orientation and clearance; CENTER centers the subject between two references along chosen axis; and SNAP translates it along specified direction until it reaches support at the prescribed gap. The SDK resolves the anchors in shared coordinate frame and computes the rotation and translation required by the selected relation, preserving pose components that the operation does not constrain. Operations can be composed, for example, to center shelf between side panels and then seat it against the back panel. Changes to the underlying geometry automatically propagate through these relationships, keeping dependent placements consistent without manually recomputing coordinates. A.2 AGENT TOOLS Following Articrafts tool interface (Zhou et al., 2026), we expose actions for editing, execution, inspection, and reference retrieval  (Table 4)  . The Coding Agent can modify the asset program, while the Review Agent can inspect the asset and edit its own tests without changing the asset itself. Editing and execution. The Coding Agent writes or patches the construction program and can execute Blender scripts to create the corresponding geometry. Compilation builds the asset and returns diagnostics for invalid structure, disconnected geometry, unintended overlaps, and failed tests. The Review Agent separately writes and revises tests against the blueprint, then executes them on the asset to obtain failures and supporting details. Inspection. Both agents can query the part hierarchy and joint axes and limits, or run read-only probes to measure dimensions, clearances, overlaps, and connectivity. These measurements identify the parts and spatial relationships involved in suspected defect. They can also retrieve the physics evidence associated with the current asset to examine failures under articulation or gravity. Visual Inspection. request_render uses Blender to produce RGB images or semantic maps that assign distinct flat colour to each part, making part boundaries easier to distinguish. Both agents can request front, side, top, or perspective views in open or closed configurations and focus on named parts or joints. A.3 PHYSICAL SIMULATION Collision under Motion. We use MuJoCo to check collisions at sampled joint configurations, with mesh collision geometry constructed by CoACD using decomposition threshold of 0.05, at most 32 convex hulls per mesh, and random seed 0. The initial collision screen includes the rest pose, seven evenly spaced values along each joints travel, pairwise 7 7 grids, and 200 random multi-joint samples drawn from the same joint-value grids. We cap this initial set at 1,500 configurations and use sampling seed 0. The functional constraints in Qtext guide checks of dependent motions: for example, an internal drawer is tested with its access door opened, so an invalid operation sequence is not mistaken for geometric defect. Collisions that persist during individual joint operation are sent to the Coding Agent for repair. For collisions found only when multiple joints move together, the Review Agent determines whether they occur during normal use and need repair. For each affected part pair, the report records representative configuration and penetration depth, allowing the agents to reproduce and inspect the finding. Stability under Gravity. For free-standing assets, we test stability under gravity in MuJoCo at rest and with each joint opened in turn. In each test, the assembly is placed on ground plane with free root, allowing it to settle or topple. We simulate for up to 5 s, stopping early when the roots linear and angular speeds remain at most 0.02 m/s and 0.05 rad/s, respectively, for 0.4 s. Tilt is measured as the angle between the roots initial and current up directions; final tilt above 3 is flagged for review. The physics report Et records, for each pose, the final and maximum tilt, whether the assembly settled, and the simulated duration, so the Review Agent can assess the result against the assets intended use.

sections.content: we test both ways of pairing the predicted poses with the ground-truth closed and open states. For each pairing, we align both states with ICP from several initial orientations. We select the pairing with the lower alignment error across both states, retaining the original ordering when the difference is negligible. After alignment, we normalize both assets so that the longest side of the ground-truth assets closed-state bounding box has unit length. We compute each parts centroid as the mean of its sampled surface points. Hungarian matching minimizes the total Euclidean distance between predicted and reference centroids in the aligned closed state, yielding one-to-one correspondences that are reused in the open state. B.2 MATERIAL TRANSFER PROTOCOL To separate material errors from geometric incoherence, we transfer predicted materials onto the reference geometry. We use Hungarian assignment to match parts by their relative positions, shapes, and motion between the rest and open states. Within each matched part pair, component matching minimizes weighted cost combining differences in normalized centers, bounding-box dimensions and aspect ratios, and relative surface area and bounding-box volume. We transfer materials between the resulting component matches. Numeric material parameters are copied directly, while texture inputs are reduced to surface-area-weighted means because the meshes do not share UV layouts. Keeping the ground-truth geometry and joint configurations fixed, we render base-color, metallic, and roughness buffers in Blender at 5122 resolution from three viewpoints in each state. We compute PSNR over visible object interiors, excluding boundary pixels. Scores are averaged over the six images and then over objects. Table 10 reports the transferred-material scores. B.3 EVALUATION DATASETS Spatial Fidelity Evaluation Datasets. LightWheel (Lightwheel, 2025) is library of simulationready OpenUSD assets modelled by artists and released under CC-BY-NC license. Recent articulation work adopts 243 of these assets, spanning 14 categories, as an evaluation set (Li et al., 2026a;b). It contains fourteen kitchen-appliance categories, including blenders, electric kettles, range hoods, and stovetops. We sample 50 objects evenly across the fourteen categories (Figure 7a). ArtVIP (Jin et al., 2026) comprises 992 digital-twin articulated objects over 9 categories and 37 subcategories. Each asset is built by professional 3D modellers to unified standard and ships with tuned dynamic parameters, embedded modular interaction behaviours, and pixel-level affordance annotations. Its categories extend beyond kitchen appliances to furniture, fixtures, cleaning tools, stationery, storage, and mechanical equipment. This diversity challenges methods to construct wider range of geometries and mechanisms, motivating our use of ArtVIP as the main benchmark. We select 50 objects through category-stratified sampling to span diverse object types and joint counts, and refine the selection by inspecting the models and renders. Figure 7bc shows the subsets category and joint-count distributions. Table 5 lists all 50 objects using the same category grouping. Stability Evaluation Dataset. We construct 50 object prompts around common destabilization mechanisms in everyday articulated objects, such as cantilevered loads, telescoping extensions, and tilting panels, as shown in Figure 8. By varying both object categories and mechanisms, the set tests whether generated assets remain stable across diverse support geometries and joint configurations. For example, one prompt used in the benchmark reads: narrow hallway shoe cabinet with slim upright carcass and three stacked tilt-out shoe bins. Each bin rotates outward and downward on its own horizontal revolute hinge at the bottom front edge of its opening, carrying the whole bin body clear of the carcass front. Hall-furniture scale, tall and shallow with footprint barely deeper than shoe. Figure 8 shows the distributions by the destabilization mechanism (left) and the category (right). We evaluate three articulated operation tasks from RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2026) and eight from RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026), using disjoint native training and test assets and generating additional assets matched to the training distribution. RoboCasa reveals substantial difference between physical feasibility and compatibility with demonstration generation. Among 80 assets per group, 78 native assets, 76 assets generated by ARTISAN, and 31 Articraft assets pass Round 1. After Round 2, these counts drop to 61, 35, and 6, respectively. These results reveal two distinct bottlenecks. First, Articraft frequently fails physical qualification, with only 31 of 80 assets satisfying the stability and task-feasibility requirements.
